topic: Binary Counting and the Towers of Hanoi: The Hidden Logic of Recursion
target_audience: High school students interested in computer science and discrete mathematics

outline.topic: Binary Counting and the Towers of Hanoi: The Hidden Logic of Recursion
outline.target_audience: High school students interested in computer science and discrete mathematics

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Language of Bits
sections.content: Briefly introduce the binary system (base-2) as a sequence of powers of 2. Emphasize that each position in a binary number corresponds to a specific 'decision' or state.
sections.example: Visualizing 3 bits: 001 (1), 010 (2), 011 (3), 100 (4). Animation shows lights turning on/off representing the values 1, 2, and 4.

sections.title: The Towers of Hanoi Challenge
sections.content: Introduce the classic puzzle: Move a stack of N disks from Peg A to Peg C, moving only one disk at a time and never placing a larger disk on a smaller one.
sections.example: An animation of a 3-disk puzzle where a robotic squirrel tries to move the stack. Highlight the minimum steps formula: 2^n - 1.

sections.title: Mapping Moves to Binary
sections.content: Connect the binary sequence to the physical moves. Explain that the sequence of disks moved corresponds to the bit that changes in a binary counter.
sections.example: For 3 disks: Step 1 (001), Step 2 (010), Step 3 (011), etc. Animation shows the binary counter ticking up alongside the physical disk movement.

sections.title: Algorithmic Symmetry
sections.content: Demonstrate the 'Gray Code' property: exactly one bit changes per step. This mirrors the fact that only one disk can be moved at a time in the puzzle.
sections.example: A visual table overlay where the bits 1, 2, and 3 represent disk sizes. When the counter hits 4 (binary 100), the largest disk moves.

sections.title: Synthesis & Summary
sections.content: Conclude that the Towers of Hanoi is a physical representation of a binary counter. The total number of states in a 3-bit system (2^3=8) minus the zero state equals the total steps (7).
sections.example: A final infographic showing: 3 Disks = 2^3 - 1 = 7 steps. A quick summary graphic linking 'Binary Counting' to 'Recursive Problem Solving'.

storyboard.title: Prerequisite: The Language of Bits
lecture_lines: Binary numbers rely on powers of two.
Each bit represents a simple decision.
Three bits count from zero to seven.
animations: Display three empty squares side by side, labeled Bit 1, Bit 2, Bit 3.
Change color of 'Bit 1' square to #FFFF00 (yellow) to represent value 1 (binary 001).
Fade out Bit 1, change 'Bit 2' to #FFFF00 for value 2 (binary 010).
Turn on both Bit 1 and Bit 2 to #FFFF00 for value 3 (binary 011).
Turn on only Bit 3 to #FFFF00 for value 4 (binary 100).

storyboard.title: The Towers of Hanoi Challenge
lecture_lines: Never place large disks on small ones.
The minimum moves follow two to the n minus one.
A three-disk stack takes seven moves.
The puzzle reveals a recursive pattern.
animations: Display three pegs (A, B, C) and a stack of 3 disks (different colors/sizes) on Peg A.
Animate a robotic arm (or simple visual pointer) moving the smallest disk from A to C.
Display the text 'Min Steps: 2^n - 1' at the top in #FFFFFF.
Animate moving the second disk to Peg B.
Show the full stack of 3 disks moved to Peg C, final state reached.

storyboard.title: Mapping Moves to Binary
lecture_lines: Each binary count step mirrors one move.
The changing bit dictates the disk moved.
The counter maps perfectly to the puzzle.
We watch the binary counter tick up.
Physical movement aligns with abstract counting.
animations: Show the 3-disk Tower on the left and a binary counter (001 to 111) on the right.
Step 1: Move smallest disk; animate binary counter from 000 to 001.
Step 2: Move middle disk; animate binary counter from 001 to 010.
Step 3: Move smallest disk; animate binary counter from 010 to 011.

storyboard.title: Algorithmic Symmetry
lecture_lines: Exactly one bit changes each time.
Only one disk moves per step.
The largest disk moves at four.
animations: Display a 3x3 grid showing binary steps 001, 010, 011, 100.
Highlight the bit change between consecutive steps in #00FF00 (green).
Display a pointer showing: Bit 1 = Disk 1, Bit 2 = Disk 2, Bit 3 = Disk 3.

storyboard.title: Synthesis & Summary
lecture_lines: The puzzle is a physical binary counter.
Three disks require two cubed minus one moves.
Recursive problem solving is binary logic.
animations: Display text: '3 Disks = 2^3 - 1 = 7 steps'.
Draw a connection line between 'Binary Counting' and 'Recursive Problem Solving'.
Flash both concepts in #FFFF00 to signify their logical equality.
